The same truncation of an SFT delta keeps 2.5 % at rank 1 and 46.75 % at rank 90 %. It scales the rank-1 update by a scalar, but only up to about 1: performance saturates and peaks near 0.7. The coefficient is extrapolated along training time by a linear fit (norm ratio up to 2.70), not by a size sweep of the final delta. No response length, truncation or finishing rate, no matched-norm random control, no hard-subset breakdown. Its ExPO baseline (2404.16792) is the fixed-scalar amplification of a weight delta.

3. "Reasoning Relay: Evaluating Stability and Interchangeability of Large Language Models in Mathematical Reasoning", December 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.20647 (read: html v1). The same protocol shape as ours: a chain of thought is truncated at 25 / 50 / 75 % (of cumulative log-probability, not token count) and a second model finishes it, on MATH test (5,000 problems). Accuracy rises with the cut point (Gemma-3-4B prefix finished by Gemma-3-1B: 41.8 / 49.9 / 55.3 % against 68.1 % for the full chain and 36.3 % for the finisher alone). The pairs are large/small instruct models, not an RL model and its base; a weaker model's prefix finished by the stronger one is not tested; no split by prefix correctness.

Also seen in search snippets only, not read in full: arXiv 2605.16874 (abstract read: about 8 % of tokens carry the base/reasoning-model disagreement on Qwen3-0.6B and they concentrate early in the response); arXiv 2510.07364 (hybrid of base and thinking model recovers up to 91 % of the gap, from the abstract snippet); arXiv 2512.17079 and 2510.00938 (flawed or weak prefills lower accuracy on MATH-500, snippets only).
nov.what_is_new: The headline is already published: a base model finishing an early prefix of an RL (Rank-1) chain approaches RL accuracy (2510.00553, App. D), and base/RL divergence and its causal effect concentrate at the start of the response in both swap directions (2603.22446). What I found no published table for is the split by prefix correctness (RL as finisher rescues wrong base prefixes, +17.1 points at 25 % and 50 %, +5.7 at 75 %, equal on right prefixes, 83 vs 83 of 88) and the fixed-fraction 25/50/75 % two-way swap between an RLVR model and its own base on MATH-500, including RL keeping about half its edge when it takes over a base answer at the midpoint. Note that our 25 % recovery (42 %, interval includes 0, base failures mostly cap hits) is weaker than the published "first 20 tokens nearly suffice", so the page should cite that result and state the difference instead of claiming the early-location finding as new.

picks.reason: Splits errors causally by resampling from the token before the judged first wrong step: a slip is a chance event (49.2 % from the prefix against 47.6 % from scratch), while a misreading is already lost (32.1 % against 64.3 %) although the prefix shows it in only 3 of 14 cases. That is a latent commitment to a wrong problem representation before any visible evidence, and the unposted RL arm suggests RL does not inherit it. To check: only 14 misreading prefixes and one LLM judge's labels; the from-scratch baseline must be matched on problem and token budget; selection on a sample that went wrong inflates the drop (regression to the mean), so it needs the same continuation from equally early prefixes of right samples; the RL result (+9.5 [-6.5, 27.4]) is not yet significant.

Teacher-forced over 4.3 M positions, RL does not act as a critic of the base: at the base's wrong boxed answers it gives the box the same probability (median D 0.001), and D on base-wrong answers that RL solved equals D on right ones (p = 0.82). The large disagreement is a format one (-8.36 nats on an 'Answer:' line). This says the RL gain is a change in the trajectory RL writes, not error detection on a given text, which constrains every reranking or contrast-decoding use of RL. To check: n is 10 and 21 in the key cells; the wrong box may be forced by the preceding context, so D should be measured at the first wrong step too (U015 and U002 partly do this); confirm the 0.000 median is not a saturation effect of near-deterministic box tokens.

A clean self-caught instrument interaction: RL's +10.8 points when continuing base wrong-step prefixes is entirely in capped rows (42 against 9 scored right), and among continuations that ended both models have exactly 90 right. RL boxes an answer and keeps checking, and a last-box grader credits it. This is both a behavioural fact about what RL learned (commit early, verify after) and a warning for every capped comparison in the project. To check: rerun with a larger cap or a first-box grader on the headline cells, and count how much of the main RL-minus-base gap on hard328 sits in capped-but-boxed rows.

Two routes to nearly the same accuracy are orthogonal in weight space: RL-Math against the imitation (Think-SFT) delta has cosine -0.00001 (null sd 0.00013), while RL-Math and RL-Code share a direction at about 120 null sd, and cue tokens appear in late-layer readouts only for the RL deltas. Combined with Think-SFT solving 58 of the 65 RL-only problems, it is a neat case of functionally similar, geometrically unrelated solutions, measured in 111 s with no forward pass. To check: cosine 0.016 is tiny in absolute terms and the two RL runs may share optimiser, data order or quantisation artefacts (half the entries moved by one bf16 unit, U001), so the null should be two RL runs on unrelated tasks or a sign-pattern null; the Think-SFT delta is 100 times larger, so compare in the RL delta's subspace as well.

A knowing-without-acting dissociation: both models put the right arithmetic result above 0.99 before it is written and the wrong written value is absent from the layer-24 readout, yet after a planted wrong line both continue with 'So' or 'Now'; RL raises the hold-on log-prob by only 0.066 nats more than the base. So RL did not learn to act on error knowledge the base already has. To check: planted errors in synthetic chains differ from self-generated ones (teacher-forced, off-distribution text); the hold-on rise of +0.28 to +0.35 nats should be converted to an absolute probability of 'Wait', and tested on the models' own slips located in U013.

A well-controlled negative with a useful decomposition: linear probes read problem difficulty from the residual stream (AUROC 0.73 to 0.77 across problems) but cannot tell which of the base's own samples on a problem will fail (within-problem 0.51 to 0.57), and RL's log-ratio on base text is no better than answer length (0.853 against 0.855). It bounds what any early critic or probe-based restart can buy and agrees with U014's slip-is-chance result. To check: only 4 samples per problem and linear probes at three layers; a nonlinear probe or a probe at the located wrong step could still find signal, and the 0.571 at 1,000 tokens has an interval that excludes 0.5, so the claim is 'weak', not 'none'.

A replication check on a released weight-edit method: norm-matched and KL-matched random columns give 28 and 30 of 300 against the edit's 33 (base 14), so most of the published-style accuracy gain on a cap-limited model is a generic perturbation effect, while only the loop reduction is specific. The control is reusable for any 'targeted edit raises accuracy' claim, including this project's own loop-neuron edit (U022, U023). To check: 300 problems, one sample and a base at 4.7 % make the interval wide ([-1.7, 5.0]); the noise floor of U006 applies; confirm the random edits match the original's layer placement and that the released edit was reproduced at its published setting.

The best instrument check among the agent-research findings: a planted theory with every effect reversed scored as well as the real LLM-written theories on 58 backtest targets, and best on the 16 targets a theory speaks about, so the first theory-scoring round did not discriminate at all. A reversed-sign plant is a cheap control that any automated-hypothesis pipeline should carry. To check: whether the failure was noise level (noise 3), target choice or scoring rule; round 02 is reported as mostly fixed but one reversal still beat its theory (6 wins against 3), so the discriminating power needs a number with an interval over several plants.

Mechanism claim with a real twist: the 100 neurons with the largest transplant effect have base-to-RL weight cosine 1.0000, 44 of them are always-on (1 of 100 layer-matched random), and a one-sentence description picks their firing snippets blind at 90.7 % (random neurons 71.3 %). So RL acts by changing what feeds existing high-gain neurons, not by editing them, which also explains why weight-change rankings fail (U024). To check: (1) the 'transplant effect' for a neuron whose weights are unchanged must be an activation patch, so confirm the patch is not just a large-norm effect of any always-on neuron (patch norm-matched always-on neurons that are not in the top 100); (2) always-on neurons are trivially easy to describe and score, so redo the blind test only on the 56 that are not always-on; (3) trace which upstream weights move their input, and check that the effect holds on held-out positions rather than the positions used to rank them.

Method gotcha with reach beyond this project: 53.6 % of changed entries moved by at most one bf16 unit, so rounding base + a (RL - base) to nearest gives an effective a of 0.12 for 0.25 and 0.88 for 0.75; stochastic rounding restores it. Any weight-interpolation, task-arithmetic or model-diffing work on bf16 checkpoints of lightly fine-tuned models has this bias, and I have not seen it stated. It also decides how to read the blend results (U010, U011, U068). To check: recompute effective a as the projection of the rounded delta on the true delta from merge_stats.json; confirm which rounding each posted blend cell actually used (each cell's merge.json); confirm the 'one unit' count is in units of the entry's own exponent; and ask whether a 43 %-changed, 0.13 %-norm delta is itself partly bf16 rounding noise of the optimizer, by comparing against the Code-RL delta sign agreement.

An instrument failure that is specific to a model family: on Olmo-3 and OLMo-2, mean-replacing about 50 earlier-layer neurons moves an unrelated target neuron (off-target / own-fall ratio 0.163, 0.067 without always-on neurons) while Gemma and Qwen show 0.003 to 0.004, and the cause is a few dozen mid-layer neurons at about 145 times the layer median. That is a concrete warning for every mean-ablation circuit result on Olmo, and links to U026's always-on neurons. To check: 56 fake pairs is small, so rerun with more pairs and other target layers; confirm the model sizes are comparable (7B against 4B) by testing a 7B non-Olmo model; test resample ablation as well as mean and zero; and verify the outlier neurons are the same ones that feed the final normalisation rather than a tokenizer or BOS-position effect.

Clean dissociation between knowing and acting: on 300 right/wrong twin chains both models assign the right result above 0.99 before it is written and never read the wrong one in the layer-24 readout, yet after a planted wrong line both continue with 'So' or 'Now' (base 194 + 99, RL 195 + 103); the hold-on log-prob rises only 0.28 and 0.35 nats. RL does not add error detection, and the knowledge is present but not used. To check: a planted error is off-distribution from a self-made slip (U015 says real wrong steps are not unlikely tokens), so repeat on the 51 located real first wrong steps; check top-1 hides a meaningful shift by reporting P(Wait) in absolute terms; and patch the pre-error 'right result' representation into the post-error position to see whether it produces a correction.

A causal resampling result that separates two failure kinds: restarting the base from the token before a judged slip gives the from-scratch rate (49.2 against 47.6 %), but before a misreading it is already down 32 points (32.1 against 64.3 %) although the misreading is visible in the prefix in only 3 of 14. That says a misreading is a latent state set early and a slip is sampling noise, which is a probe target: something in the residual stream before the visible sentence should predict it, unlike the null within-problem probe of U002. To check: 14 prefixes is thin and the interval is [-50, -16.7], so enlarge; the judge's label and quote location define the groups, so use a second blind judge; rule out that misread prefixes are simply later or longer, by matching prefix length and problem difficulty; and follow up the unposted note that RL continuing the same prefixes does not lose.

Weight-space geometry obtained in 111 s with no forward pass: the RL-Math delta is orthogonal to the Think-SFT delta (cosine -0.00001, null sd 0.00013) although the two models score nearly the same, while RL-Math and RL-Code share a direction at cosine 0.016, about 120 null sd; cue tokens show up in late-layer readouts of both RL deltas and in 0 of 96 for Think-SFT. Two routes to the same accuracy with no shared weight direction is a good target for a causal test. To check: the Gaussian null is weak for structured deltas, so use a permuted or rotated-delta null and another same-base fine-tune as a control; a shared direction could be the shared RL recipe (optimizer, bf16 rounding from U001, weight decay) rather than a shared skill; the Think-SFT delta is 100 times larger, so orthogonality of the whole may hide alignment in its top subspace: project RL-Math onto Think-SFT's top singular directions per matrix.

A neat warning about steering as evidence of mechanism: the steering strength that makes the base write 'Wait' as often as RL puts a hold-on word in the layer-24 readout at 31 % of positions against 6.29 % in RL, five times too much, and a quarter of that strength already overshoots. Matching a behaviour by steering does not reproduce the internal state of the model that has the behaviour naturally. To check: only 63 problems; the readout is taken at the steered layer, so the overshoot may be the vector read back by the lens: measure the readout at later layers and with a lens fitted on unsteered activations, and compare at matched accuracy rather than matched Wait rate.

A matched control that deflates a released method: on Qwen3.5-0.8B the Weight-Space Programming edit scores 33 of 300 against 28 and 30 for norm-matched and KL-matched random columns (+1.7 points [-1.7, 5.0]), and is specific only on the repeated 10-gram rate. On a cap-limited model any perturbation that changes the sampling path buys accuracy, which also explains this project's own random-edit rescue in U023. To check: one sample of 300 at a 14-of-300 base is near the floor, so the interval cannot exclude a real 5-point effect: rerun with several samples and seeds, confirm the released edit was applied exactly as published (layer, scale, model revision), and repeat at a cap where the base is not cap-limited.

Claude Code puts the 5 newest commit subjects into every subagent's context, so score-bearing commit messages leak into any blind judge or predictor run inside the repo. This applies to every agent team doing blind evaluation, and the fix (headless call from an empty directory) is usable today. To check: reproduce by asking a fresh subagent to quote its context verbatim on the current Claude Code version, confirm the 7 of 68 dropped targets were really contaminated, and confirm the empty-directory run shows no git context.

Same seed under vLLM batching is a fresh sample: identical requests scored 155, 160, 164, 168 of 328, and only 8 of 328 answer texts matched between sharded and whole-cell runs. That puts a 4 to 5 point floor under every single-run comparison, which changes how any eval result should be read. To check: whether the spread is batch-composition nondeterminism alone or also hardware (H100 against H200) and vLLM version; whether the floor shrinks at T 0 or with batch size 1; and that the 4 to 5 points is not just the binomial sd restated (about 9 problems at n 328).

A three-token math prefill gives +19.3 points on 538 EvalPlus problems (41.3 % to 60.6 %), 58 % of the code RL gain, with no training. This is the most directly usable item, and also the one that sounds too good. To check: the plain base at T 1.0 is a weak baseline (plain base MATH-500 falls from 319 to 224 between T 0.6 and T 1.0), so compare against the best plain decoding setting and a generic 'think step by step' opening; check the gain is not an extraction or format effect (does the cued base just emit a parseable code block more often); repeat with several samples given the 4 to 5 point rerun floor.

RL's +10.8 point rescue from the base's wrong-step prefixes disappears when only finished continuations are counted (90 right each); the gain is 42 capped rows scored right against 9, because RL boxes an answer and keeps checking until the cap and the last-box grader credits it. A clean example of a grader and token-cap interaction producing a headline effect. To check: read the 42 capped RL rows to confirm the boxed answer is stable rather than one of several; rerun with a larger cap to see whether those rows finish right; test whether the same interaction inflates the main RL-minus-base numbers elsewhere.

A norm-matched random weight edit recovers most of a released 'loop-fix' edit's accuracy gain (28 and 30 of 300 against 33; base 14), so the published gain is mostly perturbation on a cap-limited model, with only the loop rate specific. The matched random control is cheap and reusable for any weight-edit or steering claim. To check: 300 problems and one sample leaves +1.7 [-1.7, 5.0], so it cannot rule out a real 3 to 5 point specific effect; repeat with more samples and seeds, and at a cap that does not bind, since at 14 of 300 the base is mostly measuring cap hits.

Answer length alone predicts a wrong answer at AUROC 0.831 (base) and 0.962 (RL), beating every lens feature; U079 adds that it matches a 7.37 USD LLM judge as an abstention signal. A free confidence signal for routing or abstention. To check: most of the signal is cap hits (finished-only base AUROC drops to 0.758), so report it separately for finished answers; it is partly a problem-difficulty proxy, so test within problem (U069 gives concordance 0.62 to 0.72); and test on a non-math task before relying on it.

A planted theory with every effect reversed scored as well as the real ones in the first backtest, and best on the targets it actually spoke about. This is the right kind of instrument test for any LLM-theory or auto-research scoring loop, and it shows the first round measured nothing. To check: whether round 02's discrimination (every reversal net -2 or lower) holds with more than one planted theory and on targets chosen before scoring, and whether real theories ever beat the no-theory readers, which the claim says they did not in round 01.

Across 10 sessions, 377 of 596 agent wall minutes were waiting for a person and only 47 were model time; 270 of 318 job-status calls came within 2 minutes of the previous one. It says the bottleneck in a human-plus-agents team is human response, not compute or model speed, which directs where to invest (pre-approved permissions, wait primitives). To check: how 'waiting for the person' is defined in the trace parser (idle after a finished turn is not the same as blocked on approval), and that the instrument is sound, since the related turnaround tool miscounted 395.7 of 421.7 minutes (U100).

Best dinner story: on 300 right/wrong twin chains both models give the right result p > 0.99, yet after a planted wrong line both carry on with 'So' or 'Now'. RL training barely changes this (+0.066 nats of hold-on). Knowing and acting come apart. To check: the twin stimuli are synthetic chains, so test whether it holds on the models' own natural slips; whether the 0.000 lens rate for the wrong value is a real zero or a tokenisation artifact of the readout; whether the 'hold-on' word list was fixed before the run.

Three tokens found for math (' line!\n\nOkay') lift the base on code from 222 to 326 of 538, as much as the Code model's own opening, and cover 58 % of the RL-Code gain. A cue that is about 'start thinking', not about the subject, is strange and practical. To check: one sample at T 1.0 against a 4 to 5 point rerun noise floor (U006), so it needs more seeds; a control with a random or neutral 3-token prefill; whether the plain base's 41 % is mostly format or extraction failures that the cue repairs rather than better code.

A planted theory with every effect reversed scored as well as the real theories, and best on the 16 targets a theory actually speaks about. The team's theory-scoring instrument caught itself not working, which is the kind of honesty I would tell people about. To check: whether later rounds really discriminate (round 02 still had one reversal beating its theory 6 to 3), and whether the noise setting of 3 simply swamps 58 targets, i.e. the power of the backtest.

The 100 neurons that matter most for carrying the RL change were not changed by RL at all (cosine 1.0000), are mostly always-on, and can be described in one sentence that a blind reader uses at 90.7 %, e.g. a 'Hmm / Wait at sentence start' neuron. The effect arrives from upstream. To check: the random baseline already scores 71 %, so the gap is about 19 points on 30 hand-picked 'best' neurons; always-on neurons are known to produce off-target ablation artifacts in Olmo (U057), so the transplant effect may be an instrument artifact; rerun with always-on neurons excluded.

RL moved 43 % of 7.3 billion weights, but over half of those by a single last-place bf16 unit, so asking for a 25 % blend silently gives 12 % unless you round stochastically. A whole training run living in the rounding bits is a lovely fact, and it is a trap for anyone doing weight interpolation. To check: that the released checkpoints are really stored in bf16 rather than cast on load; that the effective-a figures come from measured projected deltas and not only arithmetic; whether the dose curve in U010/U011 used stochastic rounding.

An unused column in the data pack predicts tomorrow: when a listing's intraday maximum exceeds its minimum, it has a new price next day 76 % of the time against 1.2 %, and Verda's max today is its min tomorrow 98 % of the time. Held on locked origins (6 of 6). Too good, so check for look-ahead: is the day's maximum fully known at the forecast origin, or does the collector's day boundary or time zone put tomorrow's first snapshot into today's row? The 98 % Verda figure smells like exactly that. The locked gain interval [0.008, 0.068] is also thin.

The imitation-trained model's long unfinished answers drift into Chinese (86 of 378 cap hits against 1 of 114 for RL), and it loses about 4 problems per sample because the grader rejects a right answer on the line after 'Answer:'. Fun and it changes a headline comparison in Think-SFT's favour. To check: read the Chinese text, is it continued math or noise; whether the training data has Chinese reasoning traces; regrade with a fixed, versioned grader on all models so the correction is not one-sided.

Blind tests leaked through git: the harness puts the 5 newest commit subjects into every subagent's context and the team wrote scores into commit subjects, so 7 of 68 targets had to be dropped. A small, real lesson for anyone running blind evaluations with coding agents, with a working fix. To check: only two agents were shown to have copied the lines; confirm the leak changed predictions (compare exposed against unexposed targets) and that the empty-directory headless run really carries no repo context.

More than half of RL's changed weights moved by one bf16 unit, so nearest rounding turns a 0.25 blend into an effective 0.12. That is a silent bug in any weight-interpolation or task-vector work on bf16 checkpoints, and stochastic rounding is a one-line fix. Check: recompute the one-unit share and the effective a from merge_stats.json, confirm the blends behind the posted interpolation scores (U010, U011) used stochastic rounding or float32, and confirm the effective a is a projection onto (RL - base), not an entry count.

The harness puts the 5 newest commit subjects into every subagent's context, and those subjects carried scores, so 'blind' predictions were not blind. Anyone running agent-based blind evaluation inside a repository has this leak. The fix (headless call from an empty directory) is cheap and general. Check: reproduce by asking a fresh subagent to quote its context, confirm the 7 of 68 excluded targets, and test whether the empty-directory call leaks through any other path (memory files, MCP, environment).

377 of 596 agent wall minutes went to waiting for a person and only 47 to the model: the human is the limit, not compute or model speed. 270 of 318 polling calls came within 2 minutes of the previous one. This is the number that says where a small team should invest. Check: how 'waiting for a person' is defined in the trace audit, whether sessions left open while the person slept or worked in another session are counted as waiting, and whether 10 sessions on day 1 represent the later 87.

RL's +10.8 point rescue of base prefixes disappears among continuations that ended (90 right each): the whole gain is 42 against 9 capped rows that the last-box grader scores right. A clean case of a benchmark gain produced by a grader and a stopping habit together. Check: regrade the 306 + 306 rows with capped rows counted wrong and with first-box scoring, and test whether the same interaction inflates other posted RL-minus-base gaps under grader v3.

A 4.8 M-parameter transformer trained only on simulated listing series scores +0.267 against +0.272 for the 120 M-parameter Chronos-2, with no real price in training. A domain prior written by hand in a day replaces a foundation model 25 times its size; that is cheap to copy to other sticky-price markets. Check: the simulator's listing types were read off the real providers, so confirm no evaluation-period data shaped the prior, score it on the six locked origins (only development skill is quoted), and give a bootstrap interval for the 0.005 difference.

A planted theory with every effect reversed scored as well as the real theories, and best on the 16 targets a theory actually addresses. The team ran the control that most LLM-theory pipelines skip, and it showed the backtest did not discriminate. Check: whether round 02's scoring now separates reversals reliably (one reversal still won 6 to 3), how many targets carry signal above noise 3, and whether any later round's theory beats both the null readers and its own reversal.

On clean work with nothing to fix, the skill reviewer cut a bootstrap from 1,500,000 to 10,000-20,000 resamples against the owner's written requirement, saving 7x compute and changing the tables; the plain reviewer left them intact. An optimiser told to always make one change will break a constraint when no real waste exists. Check: only 2 reviews per arm, so repeat with more arenas, and test whether a 'no change is a valid outcome' line in the skill removes the override without losing the 3.7x of U009.

A norm-matched random weight edit gives 28 of 300 against the released Weight-Space Programming edit's 33 (base 14): most of a published accuracy gain is a non-specific effect of perturbing a cap-limited model, while the edit is specific only on the repeated 10-gram rate. A cheap replication with the control the original lacked. Check: the interval [-1.7, 5.0] does not exclude a real 5-point effect, so add samples and seeds, confirm the released edit was applied as published (model, layer, scale), and test at a cap where the base is not at 14 of 300.
